title: Lifted increase (RLI and LLI)
subtitle: Near-invisible increases that lift the stitch below.
excerpt: The right lifted increase (RLI) and left lifted increase (LLI) work by lifting a loop from the row below and knitting into it. The most invisible of all increases, with no bar and no hole.
sourceNotes: Increase method documented in Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938) as the 'loop increase'. Related techniques appear in Weldon's Practical Knitter, Series 3 (1888).

glossaryTerms.definition: Right lifted increase: a right-leaning increase made by inserting the right needle into the back of the stitch one row below the current stitch on the right needle, and knitting into it.
Left lifted increase: a left-leaning increase made by inserting the left needle into the back of the stitch two rows below the first stitch on the left needle, and knitting into it.

content.text: The right lifted increase (
RLI
) and left lifted increase (
LLI

) add stitches by reaching down into the row below and lifting a stitch that is already part of the fabric onto the needle. There is no bar, no hole, and no new strand added: the lifted stitch simply spreads to accommodate the extra loop. They are widely considered the most invisible increases available. Difficulty: intermediate, as the correct stitch to lift is not always obvious at first glance.
What you need
DK yarn and 4 mm needles with several rows worked
The stitch, step by step
RLI (right-leaning, worked after the increase point):
Work to the point where the increase is needed.
Insert the right needle tip into the back of the right leg of the stitch one row below the last stitch on the right needle.
Knit into this stitch. A new stitch appears to the right of the next unworked stitch on the left needle.
Continue knitting across the row.
LLI (left-leaning, worked before the increase point):
Work to one stitch before where the increase is needed.
Insert the left needle from the back into the left leg of the stitch two rows below the first unworked stitch on the left needle.
Knit this lifted stitch. A new stitch appears to the left of the last worked stitch on the right needle.
Knit the next stitch on the left needle normally.
Where you will see it

Lifted increases appear in top-down seamless sweaters, where a paired RLI/LLI around a raglan marker gives the cleanest possible increase line. Sock gussets and thumb gussets on fitted mittens use the same pairing. Some lace shawl patterns prefer lifted increases at the edge columns because they are less visible than M1 increases.

items.symptom: Cannot find the stitch to lift
items.cause: Counting down from the wrong stitch
items.fix: For RLI: look at the last stitch on the right needle; the stitch one row below is directly beneath it. For LLI: look at the first stitch on the left needle; go two rows down.

items.symptom: Lifted stitch creates a visible hole
items.cause: Lifting the leg from the wrong direction and knitting through it untwisted
items.fix: Ensure for RLI you enter the back of the right leg, and for LLI you enter the back of the left leg. The direction of entry is what closes the hole.

items.symptom: Increase looks like a twisted stitch rather than an extra stitch
items.fix: RLI lifts one row below; LLI lifts two rows below. If the count is off by one row, the lifted stitch will look distorted.
